clue.text: Broadcast mocking animal eating grain as fodder

indicators.note: something broadcast is heard rather than read, so the word for mocking is taken as it is spoken

parts.note: wry humour is dry and mocking
gr is the standard abbreviation for grain, the old unit of weight
an ass is a donkey, here pictured eating the grain set before it

explanation.surface: A sarcastic donkey munching corn, as if broadcast on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' tells you to hear WRY, giving RYE. The donkey 'eating' grain has the grain abbreviation at its mouth, in front of it; 'as' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ryegrass is a pasture plant grown widely to feed livestock, so it is a kind of animal fodder.

clue.text: See 11
Some running of errands for dogsbody

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A junior worker whose job is running errands.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'for dogsbody' as the definition; 'for' is only a link word, so the definition is 'dogsbody' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A gofer is a junior assistant sent on menial errands, exactly what a dogsbody does.

clue.text: Topless thin torso, sporting white bloomers

indicators.note: a word without its top loses its first letter, here the opening letter of the synonym for thin

parts.note: narrow means thin or slender

indicators.note: sporting suggests frolicking about, so these letters are moved around

explanation.surface: A slim, bare-chested figure wearing white knickers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' drops the first letter of NARROW to give ARROW; 'sporting' rearranges TORSO into ROOTS. 'Bloomers' looks like underwear but means flowering plants.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrowroot plants carry small white flowers, so they are plants that bloom white.

clue.text: Rogue with second name unknown

parts.note: to call someone is to name them
y is one of the algebra letters standing for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: A villain whose middle name is a mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: SCALLY is Liverpool and north-west English slang for a young roughneck or rascal.
explanation.definitionFit: A scally is a disreputable young troublemaker in north-west English slang, a kind of rogue.

clue.text: Fatty substances put Tory leader on edge

indicators.note: in an across answer one piece put on another comes after it

parts.note: a lip is the rim or edge of something
IDS are the initials of Iain Duncan Smith, a former leader of the Conservative (Tory) party

explanation.surface: Someone puts the Conservative party leader on edge, making him nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: IDS is Iain Duncan Smith, Conservative leader 2001 to 2003, widely known by his initials. 'On edge' looks like nervousness.
explanation.definitionFit: Lipids are the chemical class of fats, oils and waxes, so they are fatty substances.

clue.text: See 27
One writing piece about male star

parts.note: a pen is the thing one writes with

indicators.note: about signals turning the word for piece round

parts.note: a gat is slang for a gun, also called a piece
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A writer composes an article about a male celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' looks like a written article but is a gun, GAT, which 'about' turns to TAG.
explanation.definitionFit: A pentagram is a five-pointed star figure drawn with continuous lines.

clue.text: Impractically theoretical medic taking round out to home by river

indicators.note: by means beside, so the river follows
taking a letter out of a word removes it; this word pairs with out to signal deletion
out completes taking...out, telling us to remove the ring-shaped letter from the medic

parts.note: a doctor is a medic
O is round, the shape of a ring
in means at home
the Aire is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A medic gives up a round of drinks to go home by the river, which seems unrealistic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking ... out' removes O from DOCTOR to leave DOCTR. The Aire is a river through Leeds.
explanation.definitionFit: A doctrinaire person applies theory rigidly regardless of practical considerations.

clue.text: Man going on board with female, in steady relationship at first

indicators.note: the female abbreviation goes in, inside the other letters

parts.note: sure means steady or firm

indicators.note: at first takes only the opening letter of relationship

explanation.surface: A man joining a company board, with a woman, in a stable relationship.
explanation.walkthrough: SURE plus R gives SURER; 'in' places F inside it. 'Going on board' suggests a company board, but the board is a surfboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A surfer is a person who rides waves standing on a surfboard.

clue.text: Girl returned to look quickly through yearly publications

parts.note: Alma is a girl's name

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the word for skimming is written backwards

parts.note: to scan a page is to look quickly through it

explanation.surface: A girl comes back to skim through the annuals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned to' reads as coming back to someone, but it reverses the word for skimming.
explanation.definitionFit: Almanacs are annual reference books with calendars, tides and statistics, published every year.

clue.text: Standard way of saying RAM must remain constant?

definitions.meaning: a standard is an established popular song, here a jazz and pop classic

definitions.text: way of saying RAM must remain constant?
definitions.meaning: a faithful ram would tell his ewe that he would ... have any other mate

explanation.surface: A computing remark that random access memory must stay fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: RAM looks like computer memory but is a male sheep; the last word of the song title sounds like ewe, his partner, so the song becomes his vow of fidelity.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is a well-known song from 1942, recorded by many singers and so a standard of the repertoire.

clue.text: Crime committed against state senator?

parts.note: the letters of treason, made high (drunk, so jumbled), give the word senator

explanation.surface: An offence against the country by one of its own lawmakers.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as wordplay, the answer says TREASON is 'high', drunk, so its letters reel into SENATOR, the clue's last word.
explanation.definitionFit: High treason is the gravest crime against one's sovereign or country, such as plotting to overthrow it.

clue.text: Badger runs through mown grass

indicators.note: the runs abbreviation passes through, inside, the dried grass

parts.note: hay is grass cut and dried
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run, doubled here for the plural

explanation.surface: A badger scurries through a hayfield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badger' looks like the animal but is the verb to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: To harry someone is to pester them persistently, the same as to badger them.

clue.text: Those wrongly taking clarinet solos, discontentedly playing

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters are performed in a new order
dis-contented means emptied of contents, so only the outer letters of solos stay

explanation.surface: Unhappy clarinettists performing their solos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discontentedly' leaves SS from SOLOS; 'playing' rearranges CLARINET plus SS.
explanation.definitionFit: Larcenists commit larceny, the theft of property, so they take things wrongfully.

clue.text: Sting involving gin and rum drunk around Geordieland?

parts.note: Gordon's is a well-known brand of gin

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the regional abbreviation
drunk means the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
Geordies come from Tyneside in the North East of England, abbreviated NE

explanation.surface: A sting operation involving gin and drunken rum somewhere around Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: Sting, the singer, was born Gordon Sumner in Wallsend, Tyneside, hence Geordieland. 'drunk' rearranges the rum to UMR before it goes 'around' the region.
explanation.definitionFit: Gordon Sumner is the real name of the musician known professionally as Sting.

clue.text: Poet from Maidenhead almost set off in posh car

indicators.note: the other pieces go in, inside, the posh car abbreviation

parts.note: RR is short for Rolls-Royce, a luxury car

indicators.note: almost means one letter short, so the end is lost

parts.note: maidenhead is an old word for the hymen

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A poet from the Thames town of Maidenhead almost setting off in a Rolls-Royce.
explanation.walkthrough: Maidenhead is a Berkshire town, but here means hymen; 'almost' gives HYME, and 'off' rearranges SET into STE.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhymester is a writer of verse, usually a minor or trivial poet.

clue.text: A rook nested in smaller species' overcrowded area

indicators.note: nested in means placed inside, as in a bird's nest

parts.note: the wren is one of the smallest bird species
R is the chess abbreviation for rook

explanation.surface: A rook builds its nest among smaller birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rook' looks like the bird among the birds, but is the chess piece R.
explanation.definitionFit: A warren is a crowded maze of narrow streets or buildings, like a rabbit warren.

clue.text: Car that only young owners treasure always starts

indicators.note: starts means the first letters of these words are taken

explanation.surface: A car that only its young owners will always cherish.
explanation.definitionFit: Toyota is a Japanese motor manufacturer whose name also denotes one of its cars.

clue.text: Southern river with very good crustaceans

parts.note: the Cam is the river through Cambridge
pi, from pious, is crossword slang for very good

explanation.surface: A southern river teeming with excellent shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Scampi are Norway lobsters, langoustines, small shellfish often eaten breaded.

clue.text: Notes drink causing muddled confusion

parts.note: me (also mi) is the third note of the sol-fa scale, so two of them are mes
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: Drink notes lead to a befuddled mix-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess-up is a botched muddle, a state of disorder and confusion.

clue.text: See 11
See 11
Essential for galop, metronome's rising speed

indicators.note: rising in a down answer means read upwards, backwards
essential means within, at the core, so the letters are in the clue words

explanation.surface: To play a galop, the metronome's rising pace is crucial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essential for' finds OPMET in 'galop, metronome's'; 'rising' turns it round. A galop is a fast 19th-century dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Tempo is the speed at which music is played.

clue.text: Computer keyboard's lead is waterproof

parts.note: a Mac is an Apple computer

indicators.note: lead means the leading, first letter of keyboard

explanation.surface: A computer keyboard's cable can withstand water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waterproof' is a noun here: a raincoat. 'Lead' looks like a cable.
explanation.definitionFit: A mack, or mac, is a mackintosh, a raincoat, which British English also calls a waterproof.

clue.text: Adult errs when drunk? Butts in here, perhaps

parts.note: A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult

indicators.note: a drunk slurs s into sh, so one s becomes sh

parts.note: to stray is to err, go off course

explanation.surface: A grown-up goes wrong when drunk and barges in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when drunk?' turns the S of STRAYS into a slurred SH, giving SHTRAYS. 'Butts' looks like interrupting but means cigarette ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashtrays are where smokers stub out cigarette ends, so butts may lie in them.

clue.text: See 15
Blame shifted, after royal subject knocked over dearest possession

indicators.note: after means the rearranged letters follow
knocked over means turned upside down, so in a down answer read backwards

parts.note: we is the royal 'we', the subject pronoun a monarch uses

indicators.note: shifted means moved about into another order

explanation.surface: Blame passes on after a king's subject knocks over a treasured object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject' looks like a citizen but is the grammatical subject, the royal WE. In Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12) the poor man's one ewe lamb is his only treasure.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewe lamb, after the biblical parable, is someone's most cherished possession.

clue.text: Article with piece about female trainspotter

indicators.note: about means around, so the article and piece surround the girl's name

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
K is the king, a chess piece
Nora is a female name

explanation.surface: An item about a woman who loves watching trains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' looks like a newspaper article but is the chess king, K.
explanation.definitionFit: An anorak is British slang for an obsessive enthusiast, typified by the trainspotter in a hooded jacket.

clue.text: Piece of cake turned up? Keep mum on!

indicators.note: turned means turned round, so the little word is reversed

parts.note: sh is the call to keep quiet
over means on top of, as on does

explanation.surface: A cake piece appears; keep silent about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of cake' looks like a slice but means an easy task. 'Keep mum' means stay quiet, not look after mother.
explanation.definitionFit: A pushover is something very easily done, as is a piece of cake.
